zufft

zufft computes fast Fourier, cosine and sine transforms in R. It bundles the BSD-licensed FFT code of ducc0, the same files and commit that SciPy uses, so it needs no system FFTW library and carries no GPL code.

  • Replaces fftwtools without FFTW. install.packages() is enough, on every platform, and the licence is MIT.
  • Fast. Faster than fftwtools on most of the benchmark grid and within 1.5 times on the rest; threads help further.
  • Familiar. Names a fftwtools user knows (fft_c2c(), fft_r2c(), fft_c2r()), the conventions of scipy.fft for axes, normalisation and cosine and sine transforms, and drop-in replacements for stats::fft() and stats::mvfft().

Installation

Install zufft from CRAN with:

install.packages("zufft")

or the development version from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zufft")

Example 

library(zufft)

x <- c(1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7)
fft_c2c(x)                       # full complex spectrum, as stats::fft(x)
#> [1]  27+0.000000e+00i  -5+5.196152e+00i   0+4.440892e-16i -11+0.000000e+00i
#> [5]   0-4.440892e-16i  -5-5.196152e+00i
X <- fft_r2c(x)                  # the non-redundant half
fft_c2r(X, n = length(x))        # and back
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

# columns of a matrix, on two threads
m <- matrix(rnorm(4096 * 64), 4096)
spec <- fft_r2c(m, axes = 1, workers = 2)
dim(spec)
#> [1] 2049   64

# cosine and sine transforms, SciPy's definitions
fft_dct(x, norm = "ortho")
#> [1] 11.0227038 -4.6508890 -1.0000000  0.4082483  0.0000000 -3.8343924
fft_dct(fft_dct(x), inverse = TRUE)
#> [1] 1 4 2 8 5 7

# fast lengths for zero-padding
fft_next_len(1009)
#> [1] 1024

Coming from fftwtools or scipy.fft

vignette("migrating-from-fftwtools") maps every fftwtools function to zufft. The one thing to remember is that zufft scales inverses by 1/n, as SciPy does; add norm = "none" for fftwtools’ (and stats::fft()’s) unscaled numbers. The scipy.fft article covers the Python side: the definitions match, and the test suite checks 2040 cases against SciPy.

Speed

Medians on an Apple M-series laptop, against fftwtools on Homebrew’s FFTW, from bench/RESULTS.md (which also has a Linux x86-64 runner):

Case zufft, 1 thread zufft, 2 threads fftwtools
1-D complex 1 048 576 11.94 ms 6.98 ms 20.47 ms
1-D real 1 000 000 6.47 ms 3.91 ms 8.95 ms
columns real 1024 × 1024 1.64 ms 898.6 µs 3.21 ms
2-D complex 2048² 38.19 ms 20.31 ms 123.25 ms
3-D complex 128³ 16.29 ms 9.20 ms 88.70 ms

zufft caches its plans, where fftwtools plans every call, and transforms of any length run in O(n log n): a prime length of 100 003 takes 6.39 ms here against 4.17 s for stats::fft().

R stores arrays column by column, so the first axis is the contiguous one. The real transforms halve the last axis listed, as SciPy does; for speed, list the first axis last, as in fft_r2c(m, axes = 2:1).

A native build is the user’s choice: CRAN’s binaries use the portable SSE2 (x86-64) or NEON (arm64) vector width. To compile for your own CPU, add this line to ~/.R/Makevars and reinstall from source:

CXX17FLAGS += -march=native

zufft_info()$simd_width then reports the width you got. On the Linux x86-64 runner of bench/RESULTS.md, where this gives AVX2, the 16384 × 64 complex column case drops from 15.39 ms to 9.17 ms and a complex prime length of 10 007 from 659.6 µs to 389.5 µs.

Licence

zufft is MIT-licensed. Its bundled ducc0 files are the “BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0-or-later” subset that SciPy vendors, used under BSD-3-Clause; inst/COPYRIGHTS lists every copyright holder. No GPL-only ducc0 code is included.
